Robyn: Tiny Desk Concert November 12, 2026 5:00 AM ET By Dora Levite , Lars Gotrich Credit: Photo: Michael Zamora/NPR There is so much humanity within Robyn 's music — not just longing and heartbreak, but absurdity, the connections and contradictions that are all part of life's panoply. Her crystal-clear voice, honed over 30 years, sparkles in this Tiny Desk. Music Interviews Robyn's first post-parenthood album is a manifesto on sensuality The 200 Greatest Songs By 21st Century Women+ Robyn Is The 21st Century's Pop Oracle Every choice here is a tender one, down to the teardrop glued to her cheek. Every move is confident, yet comes from a place of vulnerability. Most of these arrangements play up the quiet desperation in her outsized songs, though on "Ever Again," Robyn pulls off a magic trick by inviting us into the conversation, opening a broken heart to defiant resilience. "Light Up," in particular, sounds revelatory, a glitchy synth banger reborn as a piano ballad. "I was looking at you like a mirror," she sings with a catch in her throat, like an old memory surfacing for a split second, as she builds to a moment of emotional release. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes. Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team. The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome. It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top. This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place. "Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane. Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room. "There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch. (Photo courtesy of Joseph Danielson/Nevada Department of Wildlife) Tucked within eastern Nevada public lands is a haven for bats: Rose Guano Cave. Nestled in the remote landscape of White Pine County, Rose Guano Cave serves as critical habitat for one of the largest concentrations of bats in the region and provides an important stopover during migration from July through October each year. The number of bats using Rose Guano Cave fluctuates annually, with population estimates typically ranging between 1 and 3 million bats. Bats fly from Rose Guano Cave in Nevada. (Photo courtesy of Bryan Hamilton/Nevada Department of Wildlife) Rose Guano Bat Cave is perhaps best known as home to one of the largest-known colonies of Brazilian free-tailed bats ( Tadarida brasiliensis ), also called Mexican free-tailed bats , in Nevada. pages.text: RSS Feed (Really Simple Syndication) - BBC Sport Published 22 May 2024 What is RSS? In a world heaving under the weight of billions of web pages, keeping up to date with the information you want can be a drag. Wouldn't it be better to have the latest news and features delivered directly to you, rather than clicking from site to site? Using RSS (Really Simple Syndication) allows you to see when sites from all over the internet have added new content. You can get the latest headlines and articles (or even audio files, photographs or video) in one place, as soon as they are published, without having to remember to visit each site every day. RSS takes the hassle out of staying up-to-date, by showing you the very latest information that you are interested in. RSS feeds are just a special kind of web page, designed to be read by computers rather than people. It might help to think of them as the free, internet version of the old-fashioned ticker-tape news wire machines. Not all websites currently provide RSS and not all sections of the BBC or BBC Sport website are available as feeds. How do I start using RSS feeds? In general, the first thing you need is something called a news reader. This is a piece of software that checks RSS feeds and lets you read any new articles that have been added to them. There are many different versions, some of which are accessed using a browser, and some of which are downloadable applications. Close Rub21's Diary A map of open OSM notes, sorted by what they need Posted by Rub21 on 12 November 2026 in English . There are about 450,000 open notes on OpenStreetMap. Each one is a message from someone who saw a problem on the map. But to know what a note needs, you have to open it and read it, one by one. That takes a lot of time. So I trained a machine learning model to do this first read for us. I also made a simple website to show the results: → https://osm-notes.rub21.com What does the model do? The model reads the first comment of each note and gives it two labels: Category : what the mapper should do. For example: missing place, place closed or changed, wrong name, missing or wrong road, other wrong data, spam, empty, or not mappable (opinions, questions). Theme : what the note is about. For example: food, shops, health, roads, transport. How I built it The notes. Andrés ( AngocA ) built OSM-Notes-Ingestion . It loads all OSM notes into a database and keeps them up to date every minute. On top of it, I built a small pipeline that: loads the full notes dump from the planet file, takes the first comment of each note (the one that explains the problem), detects the language of each note. Training data. This was the hardest part, and it took several rounds. The AI helped me a lot, but I reviewed many of its labels: I sent about 10,000 notes to three popular AI models: Claude, GPT and Gemini. The data team at Mapbox have built tools that allow detecting and cleaning these issues as they happen on the map. Detecting issues with OSMlint To detect issues, we run spatial analysis on the map data of the whole world everyday using OSMlint . This is made possible be leveraging the power of tile-reduce to analyze OpenStreetMap vector tiles using javascript. OSMlint consists of a set of validators which check the data on each tile for common issues in geometry and tags. An example validator is crossingHighways which detects roads that cross each other without an intersection. Each validator produces a GeoJSON output of the OpenStreetMap geometries that are invalid and needs review. Fixing issues with To-fix To-fix is a micro tasking tool that helps us create tasks of issues to fix on OpenStreetMap. The issues collected with OSMlint is loaded into to-fix, each of which is then reviewed by a member of the mapping community or the Mapbox data team. Over 500,000 issues have been fixed so far using to-fix. To-fix also allows marking issues as false positives. These are later investigated and used to improve the validator algorithm in OSMlint. The linting pipeline We’ve implemented an architecture that automates the detection of issues using OSMlint and loading them into to-fix on a daily basis. Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot. "We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related." Cyber-security experts have said there is no evidence connecting the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure. In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, several US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said this was not a cyber-related incident. pages.text: Russia barred from Junior Ice Hockey World Championships in Canada - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 By Dan Roan Sports editor Published 15 November 2026 Russia's hopes of reintegration into international sport suffered a setback when it was barred from the upcoming Junior Ice Hockey World Championships in Canada. It comes despite a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) last month ordering the country's return to the competition. The hosts then said they would deny entry to Russian athletes as a result of the war in Ukraine. "Due to the position and restrictions formally communicated by the Canadian government, the Russian Under-20 national team is unable to participate in the World Junior Championship," the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement. It added that "after carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer." The Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable and unlawful" and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC). "The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons," it added. More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. He focuses on the national security side of the Justice beat, including counterterrorism, counterintelligence and transnational repression. Before joining NPR, Lucas worked for a decade as a foreign correspondent for The Associated Press based in Poland, Egypt and Lebanon. In Poland, he covered the fallout from the revelations about secret CIA prisons in Eastern Europe. In the Middle East, he reported on the ouster of Hosni Mubarak in 2011 and the turmoil that followed. He also covered the Libyan civil war, the Syrian conflict and the rise of the Islamic State. He reported from Iraq during the U.S. occupation and later during the Islamic State takeover of Mosul in 2014. He also covered intelligence and national security for Congressional Quarterly. Lucas earned a bachelor's degree from The College of William and Mary, and a master's degree from Jagiellonian University in Krakow, Poland. That said, planning is an important step in being prepared and ready for your adventure. Remember, the Monument can be very unforgiving, and its wild character should not be underestimated. And although overnight stays on the monument do not require a permit, free permits are available at any of the local Visitor Centers and are highly encouraged. The permit system can become crucial in the case of a search and rescue . Below are some best practices to keep in mind when recreating on the GSENM: It’s always a good idea to let people know your itinerary and when you expect be back Travel in groups rather than by yourself Before beginning any of your Monument adventures, make sure you've planned your way in, and planned your way out Know the extended weather forecast Carry extra clothing, blankets, food and water for emergencies Remember, cell phone coverage across the Monument is sparse if at all Plan Ahead and Prepare

pages.text: Salvador: Why 2027 Is the Year to Visit Brazil's First Capital | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD In Salvador, Immerse Yourself in Afro-Brazilian Culture The capital city of Bahia will host a particularly dynamic festival season in 2027. Acarajé da Dinha, a legendary kiosk in Salvador’s Rio Vermelho district, is renowned for its acarajé , a savory fritter made from black-eyed peas and an emblem of Afro-Brazilian culture. Luisa Dörr By Dan Stables Published October 20, 2026 Widely considered the capital of Afro-Brazilian culture, Salvador is one of the most vibrant cities in Brazil, a place where colorful Portuguese architecture meets sun-drenched beaches, with a fiery cuisine that combines tropical flavors and African influences. It is also host to one of the world's most flamboyant Carnivals, a hotbed for samba music, and the heartland of the martial art capoeira. In February 2027, for the first time in decades, Salvador Carnival will take place at the same time as Festa de Iemanjá, the major festival in candomblé—a religion that fuses Catholicism with West African religions—making this an ideal time to visit the city. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) When to Go Salvador has a tropical climate, so it's best to visit between September and February during the dry season, when there is less rainfall and more hours of sunshine. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn San Juan Islands National Monument Situated in the northern reaches of Washington State's Puget Sound, the San Juan Islands are a uniquely beautiful archipelago of over 450 islands, rocks, and pinnacles. The San Juan Islands National Monument encompasses approximately 1,000 acres of land spread across many of these rocks and islands and managed by the Department of the Interior's Bureau of Land Management. Drawing visitors from around the world, this is a landscape of unmatched contrasts, where forests seem to spring from gray rock and distant, snow-capped peaks provide the backdrop for sandy beaches. The San Juan Islands National Monument is a trove of scientific and historic treasures, a refuge for an array of wildlife, and a classroom for generations of Americans. On March 25, 2013, President Obama signed a proclamation to designate the San Juan Islands National Monument. The proclamation states that, "The protection of these lands in the San Juan Islands will maintain their historical and cultural significance and enhance their unique and varied natural and scientific resources, for the benefit of all Americans." pages.text: Santander, Spain: A 2027 Guide to Its Waterfront Art Museums | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Beloved by Spaniards, Santander Is Becoming a Global Art Mecca The easygoing beachfront city is getting a host of new and reborn museums. A 2014 transformation by landscape architect Fernando Caruncho more than doubled the size of Pereda Gardens, in the historic heart of Santander. Luis Fonseca, Getty Images By Eddi Fiegel Published October 20, 2026 Santander, a port city in northwestern Spain, has long seduced Spaniards with its spectacular horseshoe bay surrounded by rolling green hills and the Cantabrian mountains in the distance. But now the city, the capital of the Cantabria region, is poised to become an international art destination. In September 2026, the new arts, culture, and technology center Faro Santander opened in a historic building redesigned by acclaimed British architect David Chipperfield with a permanent collection including works by such legendary figures as el Greco, Rubens, Velázquez, and Goya. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) Meanwhile, 2027 will bring the first outpost of Madrid’s renowned Reina Sofía museum. The impressive Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria also has a new home designed by the Barcelona-based architecture practice Mendoza Partida. Art lovers are sure to appreciate the city’s walkable city center—where ornate, neoclassical façades sit alongside Baroque churches and grand, porticoed squares—and the wide sandy beaches lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas.

Yet you may not realize that probably the most expensive thing you will ever buy in your lifetime is your…retirement. Perhaps you've never thought of "buying" your retirement. Yet that is exactly what you do when you put money into a retirement nest egg. You are paying today for the cost of your retirement tomorrow. The cost of those future years is getting more expensive for most Americans, for two reasons. Second, you may have to shoulder a greater chunk of the cost of your retirement because fewer companies are providing traditional pension plans. pages.text: Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE Scientists find a new titanosaur dinosaur species in Patagonia The new Argentine dino might give us clues to what the world was like before the asteroid wiped out their kind. Hundreds of fossils found at a quarry in Northern Patagonia provide a snapshot of what a desert pond ecosystem might have looked like in the late Cretaceous period. Researchers found a previously undiscovered species of titanosaur (illustrated above) among other fossilized creatures at the site. Illustration by Gabriel Lio By Meghie Rodrigues Published March 5, 2025 In Northern Patagonia, paleontologists have unearthed an ancient lagoon ecosystem surrounded by sand dunes and palm trees where prehistoric creatures thrived. Excavations of 78 million year-old rocks, from a quarry just outside General Roca city in Argentina, yielded a treasure trove of 432 fossils belonging to over a hundred animal groups. The majority of the fossils belonged to turtles, but other residents were fish, crocodile relatives, slugs—including the first fossil record of the Neocyclotidae , a family of tropical land snails, and the first record of Leptinaria , a genus of small tropical air-breathing land snails—and dinosaurs . The most important find among them all: a new titanosaur called Chadititan calvoi. pages.text: Scientists Invent a Digestible, Paper-Based Battery That Can Power Swallowed or Implanted Medical Devices Skip to main content Researchers tested the battery in an RFID tag that can be rolled up in a capsule and swallowed. It can then transmit information about the digestive tract to a reader outside the body. MIT News Ingestible sensors provide a helpful way to monitor a person’s health from the inside. But finding effective ways to power them has been a challenge. They typically use either standard batteries, which contain harmful chemicals, or external sources that provide energy wirelessly. Now, scientists have created digestible, paper-based batteries that can power medical devices inside the body and eventually get broken down. The technology, described in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering on September 21, has so far been tested only in pigs. If further studies confirm its safety in humans, it could one day power all sorts of medical devices. “For many of the systems we’re developing, we need power, and we power the system through different ways,” says study co-author Giovanni Traverso , a mechanical engineer at MIT and gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, in a statement . “Often, we use batteries, so the question here was: Could we develop a battery that was bioresorbable, and then apply that across a range of application areas?” Bioresorbable Batteries for Transient Ingestible Bioelectronics Watch on The battery contains electrodes made with the metals magnesium and molybdenum, which are safe for human consumption in small amounts. pages.text: Scientists may have solved the mystery of Nanotyrannus | National Geographic SCIENCE Teen T. rex or totally different dinosaur? The debate over Nanotyrannus gets a new twist. After decades of fierce debate, researchers say fossils once thought to be juvenile T. rex actually belong to a separate, sleeker species of tyrannosaur. Nanotyrannus was long thought to be the very prey it's shown attacking in the illustration above, a young Tyrannosaurus rex . New evidence suggests it was a different class of dinosaur. Anthony Hutchings By Nicholas St. Fleur Published October 30, 2025 One of paleontology’s most polarizing problems is a teenage Tyrannosaurus rex with an identity crisis, and two scientists say they’ve solved it. In 1942, researchers from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History found the skull of a small theropod in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. After scientists classified it as the new species Nanotyrannus lancensis in 1988, the skull sparked four decades of fierce debate: Do such fossils of small and slender tyrannosaurs represent a teenage version of the fearsome T. rex , or an entirely distinct dinosaur?
